soil-hist-073.title: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault and the first experiment station
soil-hist-073.text: In 1836 a French chemist set up the first agricultural experiment station on his wife's estate at Pechelbronn in Alsace. That was some seven years before Rothamsted. Jean-Baptiste Boussingault (1801–1887) worked mainly on agricultural chemistry and plant and animal physiology from that year on. He revived the quantitative methods first used by de Saussure and is called the father of field plot technique. He made the first analysis of crops grown in a rotation and showed that soil nitrogen rises after legume crops. Plant growth, he found, is proportional to the available nitrogen, so applying phosphorus and nitrogen together gives greater growth. Can plants take up free nitrogen from the air? He answered no, laying a basis for what became the nitrogen cycle. In 1839 he was given the chair of agricultural and analytical chemistry at the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers in Paris. Liebig hailed him as a pioneer of soil and plant chemistry, and his nitrogen work prepared the way for nitrogen fertilizers.

soil-hist-006.title: Liebig's long argument over nitrogen
soil-hist-006.text: Even Liebig changed his mind about nitrogen. He claimed that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and the claim was contested for many years. In the end it held for legumes but not for other plants. The 1840 and 1842 editions of his book said the air held too little nitrogen and that nitrogen fertilizer, perhaps as ammonia, was needed. He later decided that ammonia in rain supplied enough, and argued for years against nitrogen fertilizer. His own nitrogen-poor fertilizer had no appreciable effect in a field test. By the seventh German edition he admitted mistakes and again called nitrogen fertilizer beneficial or even necessary. In 1863 he came to appreciate biological nitrogen fixation.

soil-hist-018.title: Selman Waksman finds medicine in soil microbes
soil-hist-018.text: The first antibiotic used to cure tuberculosis came out of soil research. Selman Waksman (1888–1973) was a Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist who studied decomposition by soil organisms. He wrote Principles of Soil Microbiology (1927) and Humus (1936). His 1932 lignin theory is one of three main historical theories of how humic substances form. His Rutgers team found actinomycin, streptomycin and neomycin, and he gave the word antibiotic its modern sense. His student Albert Schatz isolated streptomycin from Streptomyces griseus. Credit for the discovery was disputed: Schatz went to court in 1950 and was recognized as co-discoverer. Waksman won the 1952 Nobel Prize for the soil studies that led to streptomycin.

soil-hist-072.title: Carl Sprengel, who stated the law of the minimum first
soil-hist-072.text: The law that bears Liebig's name was first stated by someone else. Carl Sprengel (1787–1859) was a German botanist and agricultural scientist. He trained under Albrecht Thaer and then with Heinrich Einhof at Möglin from 1804 to 1808. From 1821 to 1828 he studied natural sciences at Göttingen, where he became a professor. He was the first to state the 'theory of minimum' in agricultural chemistry: plant growth is limited by the essential nutrient present at the lowest concentration. The rule is often credited to Justus von Liebig as {{ref:soil-fert-182}}, but Liebig only popularized it later. Sprengel's books include an 1839 study of manures and their action and the 1844 Die Bodenkunde, with a full guide to the chemical analysis of field soils. He founded the Academy of Agriculture at Regenwalde (Resko), where he taught and researched until his death in 1859.

soil-hist-012.title: Peter Erasmus Müller reads the forest floor
soil-hist-012.text: Peter Erasmus Müller (1840–1926), a Danish forester and naturalist, described mor humus for the first time. He called it beech peat, by analogy with sphagnum peat. His Studies on Forest Soil ran as a series in 1878–84 in a journal he had founded in 1875, the first independent Danish forestry journal. It was translated into German and French. The studies showed how plant communities and their animals shape the ground surface, as in heathland formation. His last major work, in 1924, concluded that the Danish heaths continue the tundra that arose after the ice age and were never forested like nearby land.

soil-hist-014.title: Life powered by rock: the discovery of chemosynthesis
soil-hist-014.text: Until Winogradsky's work, autotrophs, organisms that build their own organic matter from carbon dioxide, were believed to get their energy only from light. He found organisms that draw energy from inorganic compounds instead. This is chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis. His 1887 Beggiatoa work gave the first example of lithotrophy, though not of autotrophy. His nitrifying bacteria gave the first chemoautotrophy, fixing carbon dioxide into organic compounds. Organisms that oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium for energy split autotrophs into photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs. This form of metabolism is believed to occur only in prokaryotes.

soil-hist-011.title: Albert Atterberg sets the size of clay
soil-hist-011.text: Albert Atterberg (1846–1916) did his best-remembered work late, turning to soil classification and plasticity around the age of fifty-four. The Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905. He was apparently the first to set 0.002 mm as the upper size of clay particles. Finding plasticity characteristic of clay, he devised in 1911 the consistency limits named after him. Terzaghi brought them into geotechnics, and Casagrande standardized the tests in 1932. The International Society of Soil Science formally recognized his classification work at Berlin in 1913. Sweden still uses his grain size scale.

soil-hist-076.title: Albert Bernhard Frank names the fungus-root
soil-hist-076.text: A failed royal commission to develop truffle cultivation led Albert Bernhard Frank to work out the nature and development of mycorrhizae. The German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) named the mycorrhiza in an 1885 paper. It described how certain trees are nourished through a root symbiosis with underground fungi. In 1877 he had coined the term symbiosis to describe lichens. The bacterial genus Frankia is named after him.

soil-hist-022.title: Cyril Hopkins and the soils of Illinois
soil-hist-022.text: Cyril G. Hopkins (1866–1919) was an American agricultural chemist noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils. From 1894 until his death he was chemist at the University of Illinois Agriculture Experiment Station, latterly heading its Department of Agronomy. In 1896 he began the Illinois long-term selection experiment. With Hilgard, he greatly influenced Marbut's change from seeing soils as reflections of geology to recognizing soil science as distinct from geology.

soil-hist-025.title: Roy Simonson, soil surveyor and historian
soil-hist-025.text: During World War II, Roy W. Simonson mapped soils on Western Pacific islands for the Military Geology Unit. The American soil scientist (1908–2008) had trained under Charles E. Kellogg and Emil Truog. He taught at Iowa State College before joining the USDA soil survey programs. From 1953 to 1971 he was the survey's Director for Soil Classification and Correlation. In 1967 he became editor-in-chief of the journal Geoderma. He also wrote a history of US soil survey and classification from 1899 to 1970.

soil-hist-075.title: Lorenz Hiltner names the rhizosphere
soil-hist-075.text: In an April 1904 lecture, Lorenz Hiltner introduced the term rhizosphere for the soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms. The German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) helped found microbial ecology. At the Tharandt research station he studied the symbiosis of legumes with root-nodule bacteria, work that produced the first cultures of rhizobium bacteria. He also showed the importance of root nodules for the nitrogen nutrition of black alder. In 1893 he and F. Nobbe published a work titled 'Inoculate the Soil'.

soil-hist-017.title: Enrichment culture: coaxing microbes into the lab
soil-hist-017.text: Enrichment culture is a fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied. Martinus Beijerinck invented it. With his discovery of viruses, it counts as one of his two major contributions to microbiology. Early nitrification researchers, among them Warington, Winogradsky and the Franklands, could at first only enrich cultures of nitrifiers rather than isolate them pure. The method still matters: seven of the ten described anammox species are available in laboratory enrichment cultures.

soil-hist-021.title: Farmers of Forty Centuries, King's lessons from Asia
soil-hist-021.text: In 1909 Franklin Hiram King spent nine months touring Asia, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture. His book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan recounts that tour. It discussed the advantages of sustainable agriculture and warned that such practices would be vital to farming in the future. King died before it was done. His wife Carrie Baker King finished the last chapter and published the book in 1911. Lord Northbourne called it a "classic" that no student of farming or social science can afford to ignore.

soil-hist-002.title: Russian Chernozem, the book that named soils by color
soil-hist-002.text: Studying the steppe soils of the Poltava region, Vasily Dokuchaev noticed that peasants named all soils by their color. He began to use such names himself. Russian Chernozem, his most famous work, appeared in 1883 as a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia. It came out of his extensive field studies of Russian soils that year, from which he arrived at his theory of soil formation. An English translation by N. Kaner was published in Jerusalem in 1967 for the USDA and NSF.

soil-hist-015.title: The Winogradsky column, a world of microbes in a tube
soil-hist-015.text: Sergei Winogradsky devised the Winogradsky column, a technique for studying the microbes of sediments. He developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context. The column remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world.

reviews.founders-and-pioneers: Soil science grew from several roots at once. Fallou argued that soil was separate in nature from geology, and Dokuchaev saw it as a natural body shaped by climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age; Glinka and Marbut then carried those ideas into English and into a national US classification, which Guy Smith later developed into Soil Taxonomy. Chemists such as Sprengel, Liebig, Boussingault and Lawes asked what plants take from soil, from the law of the minimum to superphosphate and the long argument over nitrogen. Microbiologists such as Winogradsky, Beijerinck, Hiltner and Waksman showed that much of soil's chemistry is the work of living things. Jenny, Richards, Bennett and Lal turned the field toward equations, measurement and the conservation and restoration of soil itself.
